{{short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{Group theory sidebar |Discrete}}
In [[group theory]], more precisely in [[geometric group theory]], a '''hyperbolic group''', also known as a ''word hyperbolic group'' or ''Gromov hyperbolic group'', is a finitely generated [[group (mathematics)|group]] equipped with a [[word metric]] satisfying certain properties abstracted from classical [[hyperbolic geometry]]. The notion of a hyperbolic group was introduced and developed by {{harvs|first=Mikhail|last=Gromov|year=1987|author-link=Mikhail Gromov (mathematician)|txt=yes}}. The inspiration came from various existing mathematical theories: hyperbolic geometry but also low-dimensional topology (in particular the results of [[Max Dehn]] concerning the [[fundamental group]] of a hyperbolic [[Riemann surface]], and more complex phenomena in [[3-manifold|three-dimensional topology]]), and [[combinatorial group theory]]. In a very influential (over 1000 citations<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gromov |first1=Mikhail  |editor1-last=Gersten |editor1-first=S.M. |chapter=Hyperbolic Groups|title=Essays in Group Theory. Mathematical Sciences Research Institute Publications, vol 8. |date=1987 |publisher=Springer |location=New York, NY |pages=75–263 |ref=Gromov_1987 |url=https://www.ams.org/mathscinet-getitem?mr=919829}}</ref>) chapter from 1987, Gromov proposed a wide-ranging research program. Ideas and foundational material in the theory of hyperbolic groups also stem from the work of [[George Mostow]], [[William Thurston]], [[James W. Cannon]], [[Eliyahu Rips]], and many others.

== Definition ==

Let <math>G</math> be a finitely generated group, and <math>X</math> be its [[Cayley graph]] with respect to some finite set <math>S</math> of generators. The set <math>X</math> is endowed with its [[Distance (graph theory)|graph metric]] (in which edges are of length one and the distance between two vertices is the minimal number of edges in a path connecting them) which turns it into a [[length space]]. The group <math>G</math> is then said to be ''hyperbolic'' if <math>X</math> is a [[δ-hyperbolic space|hyperbolic space]] in the sense of Gromov. Shortly, this means that there exists a <math>\delta > 0</math> such that any geodesic triangle in <math>X</math> is  <math>\delta</math>-slim, as illustrated in the figure on the right (the space is then said to be <math>\delta</math>-hyperbolic).

A priori this definition depends on the choice of a finite generating set <math>S</math>. That this is not the case follows from the two following facts:

*the Cayley graphs corresponding to two finite generating sets are always [[Quasi-isometry|quasi-isometric]] one to the other;
*any geodesic space which is quasi-isometric to a geodesic Gromov-hyperbolic space is itself Gromov-hyperbolic.

Thus we can legitimately speak of a finitely generated group <math>G</math> being hyperbolic without referring to a generating set. On the other hand, a space which is quasi-isometric to a <math>\delta</math>-hyperbolic space is itself <math>\delta'</math>-hyperbolic for some <math>\delta' > 0</math> but the latter depends on both the original <math>\delta</math> and on the quasi-isometry, thus it does not make sense to speak of <math>G</math> being <math>\delta</math>-hyperbolic.

=== Remarks ===

The [[Švarc–Milnor lemma]]{{sfn|Bowditch|2006|loc=Theorem 3.6}} states that if a group <math>G</math> acts [[Group action (mathematics)#Remarkable properties of actions|properly discontinuously]] and with compact quotient (such an action is often called ''geometric'') on a proper length space <math>Y</math>, then it is finitely generated, and any Cayley graph for <math>G</math> is quasi-isometric to <math>Y</math>. Thus a group is (finitely generated and) hyperbolic if and only if it has a geometric action on a proper hyperbolic space.

If <math>G' \subset G</math> is a subgroup with finite index (i.e., the set <math>G/G'</math> is finite), then the inclusion induces a quasi-isometry on the vertices of any locally finite Cayley graph of <math>G'</math> into any locally finite Cayley graph of <math>G</math>. Thus <math>G'</math> is hyperbolic if and only if <math>G</math> itself is. More generally, if two groups are [[Commensurability (group theory)|commensurable]], then one is hyperbolic if and only if the other is.

== Examples ==

=== Elementary hyperbolic groups ===

The simplest examples of hyperbolic groups are [[finite groups]] (whose Cayley graphs are of finite diameter, hence <math>\delta</math>-hyperbolic with <math>\delta</math> equal to this diameter).

Another simple example is given by the infinite cyclic group <math>\Z</math>: the Cayley graph of <math>\Z</math> with respect to the generating set <math>\{ \pm 1 \}</math> is a line, so all triangles are line segments and the graph is <math>0</math>-hyperbolic. It follows that any group which is [[Virtually cyclic group|virtually cyclic]] (contains a copy of <math>\Z</math> of finite index) is also hyperbolic, for example the [[infinite dihedral group]].

Members in this class of groups are often called ''elementary hyperbolic groups'' (the terminology is adapted from that of actions on the hyperbolic plane).

=== Free groups and groups acting on trees ===

Let <math>S = \{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}</math> be a finite set and <math>F</math> be the [[free group]] with generating set <math>S</math>. Then the Cayley graph of <math>F</math> with respect to <math>S</math> is a locally finite [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] and hence a 0-hyperbolic space. Thus <math>F</math> is a hyperbolic group.

More generally we see that any group <math>G</math> which acts properly discontinuously on a locally finite tree (in this context this means exactly that the stabilizers in <math>G</math> of the vertices are finite) is hyperbolic. Indeed, this follows from the fact that <math>G</math> has an invariant subtree on which it acts with compact quotient, and the Svarc—Milnor lemma. Such groups are in fact virtually free (i.e. contain a finitely generated free subgroup of finite index), which gives another proof of their hyperbolicity.

An interesting example is the [[modular group]] <math>G = \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)</math>: it acts on the tree given by the 1-skeleton of the associated [[Modular group#Tessellation of the hyperbolic plane|tessellation of the hyperbolic plane]] and it has a finite index free subgroup (on two generators) of index 6 (for example the set of matrices in <math>G</math> which reduce to the identity modulo 2 is such a group). Note an interesting feature of this example: it acts properly discontinuously on a hyperbolic space (the [[hyperbolic plane]]) but the action is not cocompact (and indeed <math>G</math> is ''not'' quasi-isometric to the hyperbolic plane).

=== Fuchsian groups ===

{{main article|Fuchsian group}}

Generalising the example of the modular group a [[Fuchsian group]] is a group admitting a properly discontinuous action on the hyperbolic plane (equivalently, a discrete subgroup of <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)</math>). The hyperbolic plane is a <math>\delta</math>-hyperbolic space and hence the Svarc—Milnor lemma tells us that cocompact Fuchsian groups are hyperbolic.

Examples of such are the [[fundamental group]]s of [[Surface (topology)#Closed surfaces|closed surfaces]] of negative [[Euler characteristic]]. Indeed, these surfaces can be obtained as quotients of the hyperbolic plane, as implied by the Poincaré—Koebe [[Uniformisation theorem#Geometric classification of surfaces|Uniformisation theorem]].

Another family of examples of cocompact Fuchsian groups is given by [[Triangle group#The hyperbolic case|triangle groups]]: all but finitely many are hyperbolic.

=== Negative curvature ===

Generalising the example of closed surfaces, the fundamental groups of compact [[Riemannian manifold]]s with strictly negative [[sectional curvature]] are hyperbolic. For example, cocompact [[lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattices]] in the [[orthogonal]] or [[unitary group|unitary]] group preserving a form of signature <math>(n,1)</math> are hyperbolic.

A further generalisation is given by groups admitting a geometric action on a [[CAT(k) space]], when <math>k</math> is any negative number.<ref>for a proof that this includes the previous examples see https://lamington.wordpress.com/2012/10/17/upper-curvature-bounds-and-catk/</ref> There exist examples which are not commensurable to any of the previous constructions (for instance groups acting geometrically on hyperbolic [[Building (mathematics)|buildings]]).

=== Small cancellation groups ===

{{main article|Small cancellation theory}}

Groups having presentations which satisfy [[Small cancellation theory|small cancellation]] conditions are hyperbolic. This gives a source of examples which do not have a geometric origin as the ones given above. In fact one of the motivations for the initial development of hyperbolic groups was to give a more geometric interpretation of small cancellation.

=== Random groups ===

{{main article|Random group}}

In some sense, "most" finitely presented groups with large defining relations are hyperbolic. For a quantitative statement of what this means see [[Random group]].

=== Non-examples ===

*The simplest example of a group which is not hyperbolic is the [[free abelian group|free rank 2 abelian group]] <math>\mathbb Z^2</math>. Indeed, it is quasi-isometric to the [[Euclidean plane]] which is easily seen not to be hyperbolic (for example because of the existence of [[Homothetic transformation|homotheties]]).
* More generally, any group which contains <math>\Z^2</math> as a [[subgroup]] is not hyperbolic.{{sfn|Ghys|de la Harpe|1990|loc=Ch. 8, Th. 37}}{{sfn|Bridson|Haefliger|1999|loc=Chapter 3.Γ, Corollary 3.10.}} In particular, [[lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattices]] in higher rank [[semisimple Lie group]]s and the [[fundamental group]]s <math>\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)</math> of nontrivial [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] complements fall into this category and therefore are not hyperbolic. This is also the case for [[mapping class group]]s of closed hyperbolic surfaces.
* The [[Baumslag–Solitar group]]s ''B''(''m'',''n'') and any group that contains a subgroup isomorphic to some ''B''(''m'',''n'') fail to be hyperbolic (since ''B''(1,1) = <math>\Z^2</math>, this generalizes the previous example).
* A non-uniform lattice in a rank 1 simple Lie group is hyperbolic if and only if the group is [[Isogeny|isogenous]] to <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\R)</math> (equivalently the associated symmetric space is the hyperbolic plane). An example of this is given by [[Hyperbolic link|hyperbolic]] [[knot group]]s. Another is the [[Bianchi group]]s, for example <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\sqrt{-1})</math>.

== Properties ==

=== Algebraic properties ===

*Hyperbolic groups satisfy the [[Tits alternative]]: they are either virtually solvable (this possibility is satisfied only by elementary hyperbolic groups) or they have a subgroup isomorphic to a nonabelian free group.
*Non-elementary hyperbolic groups are not [[Simple group|simple]] in a very strong sense: if <math>G</math> is non-elementary hyperbolic then there exists an infinite subgroup <math>H \triangleleft G</math> such that <math>H</math> and <math>G/H</math> are both infinite.
*It is not known whether there exists a hyperbolic group which is not [[Residually finite group|residually finite]].

=== Geometric properties ===

*Non-elementary (infinite and not virtually cyclic) hyperbolic groups have always exponential [[Growth rate (group theory)|growth rate]] (this is a consequence of the Tits alternative).
*Hyperbolic groups satisfy a linear [[Dehn_function#Isomperimetric_function|isoperimetric inequality]].{{sfn|Bowditch|2006|loc=(F4) in paragraph 6.11.2}}

=== Homological properties ===

*Hyperbolic groups are always [[Presentation of a group|finitely presented]]. In fact one can explicitly construct a complex (the [[Rips complex]]) which is [[Contractible space|contractible]] and on which the group acts geometrically{{sfn|Ghys|de la Harpe|1990|loc=Chapitre 4}} so it is of [[Finiteness properties of groups|type ''F''<sub>∞</sub>]]. When the group is torsion-free the action is free, showing that the group has finite [[cohomological dimension]].
*In 2002, I. Mineyev showed that hyperbolic groups are exactly those finitely generated groups for which the comparison map between the [[bounded cohomology]] and [[Group cohomology|ordinary cohomology]] is surjective in all degrees, or equivalently, in degree 2.{{sfn|Mineyev|2002}}

=== Algorithmic properties ===

*Hyperbolic groups have a solvable [[word problem for groups|word problem]]. They are [[biautomatic group|biautomatic]] and [[automatic group|automatic]].{{sfn|Charney|1992}} Indeed, they are [[automatic group|strongly geodesically automatic]], that is, there is an automatic structure on the group, where the language accepted by the word acceptor is the set of all geodesic words.
*It was shown in 2010 that hyperbolic groups have a [[Decidability (logic)|decidable]] marked isomorphism problem.{{sfn|Dahmani|Guirardel|2011}} It is notable that this means that the isomorphism problem, orbit problems (in particular the conjugacy problem) and Whitehead's problem are all decidable.
*Cannon and Swenson have shown that hyperbolic groups with a 2-sphere at infinity have a natural [[finite subdivision rule|subdivision rule]].{{sfn|Cannon|Swenson|1998}} This is related to [[Cannon's conjecture]].

== Generalisations ==

=== Relatively hyperbolic groups ===

{{main article|Relatively hyperbolic group}}

[[Relatively hyperbolic group]]s are a class generalising hyperbolic groups. ''Very'' roughly{{sfn|Bowditch|2012}} <math>G</math> is hyperbolic relative to a collection <math>\mathcal G</math> of subgroups if it admits a (''not necessarily cocompact'') properly discontinuous action on a proper hyperbolic space <math>X</math> which is "nice" on the boundary of <math>X</math> and such that the stabilisers in <math>G</math> of points on the boundary are subgroups in <math>\mathcal G</math>. This is interesting when both <math>X</math> and the action of <math>G</math> on <math>X</math> are not elementary (in particular <math>X</math> is infinite: for example every group is hyperbolic relatively to itself via its action on a single point!).

Interesting examples in this class include in particular non-uniform lattices in rank 1 semisimple [[Lie group]]s, for example fundamental groups of non-compact hyperbolic manifolds of finite volume. Non-examples are lattices in higher-rank Lie groups and mapping class groups.

=== Acylindrically hyperbolic groups ===

An even more general notion is that of an acylindrically hyperbolic group.{{sfn|Osin|2016}} Acylindricity of an action of a group <math>G</math> on a metric space <math>X</math> is a weakening of proper discontinuity of the action.<ref>In some detail: it asks that for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> there exist <math>R, N > 0</math> such that for every two points <math>x, y \in X</math> which are at least <math>R</math> apart there are at most <math>N</math> elements <math>g \in G</math> satisfying <math>d(x, gx) < \varepsilon</math> and <math>d(y, gy) < \varepsilon </math>.</ref>

A group is said to be acylindrically hyperbolic if it admits a non-elementary acylindrical action on a (''not necessarily proper'') Gromov-hyperbolic space. This notion includes mapping class groups via their actions on [[curve complex]]es. Lattices in higher-rank Lie groups are (still!) not acylindrically hyperbolic.

=== CAT(0) groups ===

In another direction one can weaken the assumption about curvature in the examples above: a ''CAT(0) group'' is a group admitting a geometric action on a [[CAT(0) space]]. This includes [[Space group|Euclidean crystallographic groups]] and uniform lattices in higher-rank Lie groups.

It is not known whether there exists a hyperbolic group which is not CAT(0).<ref>{{cite web |title=Are all δ-hyperbolic groups CAT(0)? |date=February 10, 2015 |work=[[Stack Exchange]] |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/1141526 }}</ref>
